name: Water level sensor module
description: Resistive water level / rain sensor: ten interleaved exposed copper traces (five fed from + through 100 Ω, five to the base of an S8050 NPN transistor) and an emitter follower whose emitter, loaded by 100 Ω to ground, is the S output. Dry, S is 0 V; as more of the traces are covered by water, base current and the S voltage rise, up to about V(+) − 0.7 V. The output depends on how conductive the water is, so it is not calibrated in mm. Runs on 3.3–5 V, under about 25 mA. Sold as: common red "Water Level Sensor" module with an S8050 transistor (3-pin header: S, +, -, 40 x 16 mm trace area), as in Elegoo/Arduino starter kits.
eli5: A strip of bare metal fingers you dip in water. The deeper the water, the higher the voltage on its S pin, so your board can tell how full a cup or tank is.

pins.name: S
pins.description: Signal (pin 1): analog output, the S8050 emitter loaded by 100 Ω. 0 V dry, rising with water level up to about V(+) − 0.7 V. Connect to an ADC pin.
Supply (pin 2), 3.3–5 V. On an ESP32 or Pico use 3.3 V so S stays below 3.3 V.

supplierQuery: water level sensor module S + - red 3 pin
buildNotes: Header order, left to right with the traces pointing down and the parts facing you: S, +, - (printed on the board).
Power + from 3.3 V on an ESP32 or Pico. S can rise to about V(+) − 0.7 V, so on 5 V it can reach about 4.3 V, which is too much for a 3.3 V ADC pin.
Only the bare traces may touch water. Keep the header, transistor and LED end dry.

Constant power under water corrodes the traces quickly. To power it only while reading, switch + with a transistor; drive it straight from a GPIO only if the pin can source about 25 mA (fully wet at 3.3 V).

The reading depends on the water's conductivity (tap, rain, distilled water all differ) and is not linear in depth. Record S dry and at your 'full' mark and calibrate against those (driver: calibrate(), level()).
On the ESP32 use an ADC1 pin (GPIO32–39) with 11 dB attenuation; ADC2 stops working while Wi-Fi is on.

example.code:
from waterlevel import WaterLevel
import time

sensor = WaterLevel({S})
while True:
    v = sensor.voltage()
    print('S=%.2fV %s' % (v, 'wet' if v > 0.2 else 'dry'))
    time.sleep(1)

test.title: Reports the S voltage set on the slider and that the sensor is wet

library.note: Passed the Sparkbench part check in simulation and matched an independent datasheet reading. Not yet tested on real hardware.
